name: The Fisk household — a reconstructed boatman (north division)
head: inf_boatman_north_03

arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL, A BOUND. Nothing dates a hypothesised household, and a year would be a claim nobody made. `not_later_than` the scene date states the only thing the inference carries: the town's need is measured on 1 July 1835, so the household is posited as being here by then and at no stated time before it.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: Not claimed. Where a hypothesised resident came from is unknowable by construction, and the documented layer's origins (Vermont, Washington, Ann Arbor) are evidence about those men and not a distribution to sample from.

reason_for_coming.note: Not claimed for the person. The reason the HOUSEHOLD is in the dataset is the trade argument in research_note, which is a statement about the town and not about a motive.

lives_at.note: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. inf_boatman_cabin_north is a structure record this parcel raises for the purpose, because no roof of the right family stood free in this district. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.

works_at.note: NO SEPARATE WORKPLACE. A boatman in this town worked in other people's buildings, in the street, or in the dwelling itself, and inventing a shop for the sake of a link would be inventing a building.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.note: HYPOTHESISED, AND NOT A PERSON. No source names this resident and none is claimed to: the record asserts that a town of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings held at least this many households of this trade, and asserts nothing whatever about any individual. THE NAME IS INVENTED TOO, and `name_basis` beside it says so and says which pool it came from: this record used to carry a bare designation instead, on the reasoning that a surname would make it look like the documented layer, but a town of designations does not read as a town and the grade, this note and name_basis all say plainly which layer this is. name_basis.note: THE NAME IS INVENTED. No source names this resident, and this field is not a finding about anybody — it is a label so that a reconstructed household reads as a household rather than as a row in a table. It was drawn from the New England and New York pool in data/reconstruction/1835_invented_name_pools.json, which is seeded from the names of the 76 ATTESTED residents this project holds — real people, named from cited sources — so that an invented resident is named the way this town's documented residents were actually named rather than the way a story would name one. The draw was weighted toward this community ON EVIDENCE: The carrying trade of the Chicago river and the lake shore was worked by the French colonial and metis community this dataset attests here, whose families - Beaubien among them - are documented in exactly this trade at Detroit, Milwaukee and Chicago. The evidence for the pool itself: The dominant documented group in this dataset by a wide margin. Attested origins among the named residents include Vermont (three households), Washington County Vermont, Burlington, Connecticut by way of Detroit, Sackett's Harbor New York, Guilford Vermont, and 'New England'. Attested surnames of this stock in the town include Harmon, Taylor, Brown, Davis, Porter, Wright, Blodgett, Carpenter, Carver, Caton, Calhoun, Peck, Dole, Newberry and Bates.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - third of 3 boatman households in this layer, in the north division. The harbour cut of 1834 opened the river to lake craft, and this dataset models both piers, two warehouses and a forwarding trade. Cargo still moved between ship and shore in lighters and Mackinac boats, and up the branches in flat-boats. Three boatman households are inferred, on the water side of the town. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one.
